screens.title: Pilot Light and Warm Standby
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn two practical AWS disaster recovery strategies that sit between full cold backup and fully active multi-region setups. Pilot Light keeps core data and artifacts replicated to a secondary region while compute is launched on demand; Warm Standby runs a minimally scaled, working version of your application in the DR region that you can scale up quickly. We'll look at the specific services you rely on — cross-region RDS replicas, DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 replication, AMIs, CloudFormation templates, Auto Scaling, and Route 53 failover routing — and how they change recovery time objective and recovery point objective trade-offs. You will see concrete CLI examples for stack creation, autoscaling updates, and Route 53 change batches, and learn common mistakes such as out-of-sync templates or failing to test end-to-end. By the end, you should be able to choose which strategy fits an application's RTO/RPO targets and budget, know the activation steps for each approach, and understand which parts of your architecture must be continuously replicated. Consider how short your acceptable outage window is, then ask: is it worth paying for always-on compute in the DR region, or do I accept a slightly longer activation for much lower cost?

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Pilot Light and Warm Standby
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Pilot Light vs Warm Standby

Understand activation steps, key AWS services, and the RTO/RPO versus cost trade-offs that guide your DR choice.

In this lesson
  • How Pilot Light keeps data and templates ready and launches compute on demand.
  • How Warm Standby keeps a minimal, running copy and the steps to scale it up.
  • Route 53 failover basics and automated activation commands.
Coming up
  • CLI examples for CloudFormation, Auto Scaling, and Route 53.
  • Common pitfalls and CI/CD synchronization for DR assets.
Data
Cross-region replication for RDS, DynamoDB, S3.
Provisioning
AMIs and CloudFormation templates ready in DR.
Failover
Route 53 failover routing and health checks.
Concept Map
Core idea
Pilot Light: data + templates ready; compute off. Warm Standby: minimal production-capable stack running.
RTO: Pilot Light tens of minutes; Warm Standby minutes. RPO depends on replication.
Common pitfalls: outdated CloudFormation, untested failovers, configuration drift.
Quick example
A Pilot Light keeps an RDS read replica and copies AMIs to the DR region; on failure you create the stack from your CloudFormation template and update Route 53 to point at the new ALB.

First, you will design and implement a Pilot Light architecture, which means you must know how to create AMIs, store CloudFormation templates in the DR region, and set up continuous data replication for services like RDS or DynamoDB. Second, you'll design and implement a Warm Standby setup: that includes provisioning and maintaining a scaled-down, running application in the DR region and knowing how to scale it up quickly. Third, you'll compare RTO, RPO, and cost trade-offs between the two strategies so you can recommend the right approach for an application's recovery targets. Fourth, you'll configure Route 53 failover routing with health checks so that DNS automatically redirects traffic to the DR region when the primary fails. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency during a drill or in hands-on labs.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Objective Details
Milestone checklist
  • Pilot Light: RDS read replica present, AMIs copied, CloudFormation templates stored, activation runbook tested.
  • Warm Standby: Minimal ASG running, secondary DB promoted path validated, scale-up tested under load.
  • Route 53: Health checks configured, failover record set created, TTLs and EvaluateTargetHealth set appropriately.
  • CI/CD: Pipeline copies AMIs and updates templates in DR region to avoid drift.
Verification mnemonic
Sync, Test, Promote — keep configuration synchronized, run full tests, and promote read replicas during drills. This three-step mnemonic helps ensure readiness.

screens.title: What is Pilot Light?
screens.narratorSegment: Pilot Light is a disaster recovery approach where you keep the minimal, critical pieces of your system always ready in the DR region while leaving the bulk of compute turned off to save cost. The key claim is simple: continuously replicate your essential data services and keep deployment artifacts ready, then launch compute and networking on demand during an incident. A concrete example is keeping an Amazon RDS read replica in the DR region or using DynamoDB Global Tables to keep data synchronized, while AMIs and CloudFormation templates for application servers are copied and available. When the primary region fails, you promote the replica or restore from replicated snapshots, create the application stack from templates, launch EC2 instances from the AMIs, and update Route 53 to route traffic to the newly created ALB. A common misconception is that Pilot Light is a backup schedule; it is not. Backups are point-in-time copies, while Pilot Light requires continuous replication and pre-built infrastructure artifacts so activation is deliberate and time-bounded. In practice you must automate AMI creation and template synchronization, and run regular drills to validate that the runbook performs as expected. Think of Pilot Light as holding the spark and tools in place so you can light the full furnace quickly when needed.

keyIdea.text: Pilot Light: data replicated and infrastructure-as-code available; compute launched on-demand to balance cost and recovery.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is Pilot Light?
Definition
Pilot Light keeps core data services and deployment artifacts in a DR region ready for activation while compute remains off to reduce cost.
Why it matters
It strikes a balance: much lower cost than always-on DR, but faster recovery than cold restore because data and AMIs are already present.
Key Takeaway

Pilot Light lowers cost by not running compute, but requires automation and tested activation runbooks to meet RTO targets.

Activation steps (conceptual)
1. Data
Ensure continuous replication: RDS read replica or DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 cross-region replication.
2. Artifacts
Create and copy AMIs; store CloudFormation templates in the DR region.
3. Launch
Run CloudFormation to create ASGs, ELBs and attach to replicated DB; update Route 53 to point to DR ALB.
Concrete example
# Example: CloudFormation stack creation in DR region
aws cloudformation create-stack \
  --stack-name MyPilotLightAppStack \
  --template-body file://app-stack.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=DBEndpoint,ParameterValue=my-dr-rds-endpoint.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com \
  --region us-east-1
This command launches the pre-defined infrastructure in the DR region and points it at the replicated database endpoint so applications start using DR data after promotion.
Common mistake
Not keeping AMIs and templates synchronized with production. If artifacts are stale, activation can fail or produce inconsistent behavior.

screens.title: Pilot Light Activation Workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Activating a Pilot Light setup is a coordinated set of steps that must be automated where possible. The flow begins with ensuring data is ready — promote a read replica or restore a recent cross-region snapshot so your DR database is a writable primary. Next, deploy the pre-stored CloudFormation template which creates the compute, networking, and load balancing resources. Launch EC2 instances from your pre-built AMIs so configuration and dependencies are already installed. Once instances are registered with the new Application Load Balancer, update environment variables and connection strings to point to the DR database endpoint. Finally, update Route 53 failover records so traffic resolves to the DR ALB. A concrete CLI example from the chapter shows creating a CloudFormation stack using an app-stack. yaml template and then applying a Route 53 change-batch that UPSERTs A records pointing to the DR ALB. A common misconception is that you can skip DNS TTL tuning; without short TTLs and proper EvaluateTargetHealth settings, clients may continue to hit the failed primary. Always include a post-activation verification step: smoke tests and health checks to ensure the application is fully operational before declaring recovery complete.

keyIdea.title: Activation steps
keyIdea.text: Promote data, deploy infrastructure-as-code, launch AMI-based instances, update connection strings, and switch DNS via Route 53.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Activation Workflow
Step-by-step
1
Promote or restore replicated data
Promote RDS read replica or restore cross-region snapshot so the DR region has a writable database.
2
Deploy infrastructure
Run CloudFormation/Terraform templates stored in the DR region to create ASGs, ALBs, security groups.
3
Launch compute from AMIs
Use pre-copied AMIs so instances boot already configured with app dependencies and configuration tools.
4
Update DNS and verify
Update Route 53 failover records to point at the DR ALB, then run health checks and smoke tests to confirm service integrity.
CLI examples
# Create CloudFormation stack in DR region
aws cloudformation create-stack \
  --stack-name MyPilotLightAppStack \
  --template-body file://app-stack.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=DBEndpoint,ParameterValue=my-dr-rds-endpoint.us-east-1.rds.amazonaws.com \
  --region us-east-1
# Route 53 change-batch example (see change-batch.json pattern in chapter)
aws route53 change-resource-record-sets \
  --hosted-zone-id Z1234567890ABCDEF \
  --change-batch file://change-batch.json
Practical tip
Use short DNS TTLs for application records and set EvaluateTargetHealth to true so Route 53 respects ALB health checks during failover.

screens.title: Automating AMIs and CloudFormation for DR
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable Pilot Light or Warm Standby depends on up-to-date AMIs and infrastructure-as-code templates in the DR region. Automation in your CI/CD pipeline should produce AMIs when application builds succeed and then copy those AMIs to the DR region, and also update CloudFormation templates or S3-stored artifacts that the DR stack will read. The chapter emphasizes that failing to synchronize templates or AMIs is a common cause of DR activation failure. Concretely, your pipeline can run image creation, then run a cross-region copy, and finally upload or version the CloudFormation template in the DR bucket. A test you should automate is launching an instance from the DR AMI periodically and running an application smoke test. That verifies both the AMI content and the networking/security settings. A misconception is assuming that copying AMIs is sufficient: you must also ensure IAM roles, parameter store entries, and environment variables needed in the DR region are kept in sync. The practical result is a runbook that states: build AMI, copy AMI to DR, update template S3 version, and run a test launch — all triggered automatically by a successful mainline release.

keyIdea.title: Artifact hygiene
keyIdea.text: Automate AMI creation and template synchronization to eliminate configuration drift and ensure successful DR activation.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › AMIs & IaC Automation
Why automate
Manual copying causes drift. Automation ensures that each release produces a DR artifact set you can confidently deploy during activation.
Pipeline steps
  1. Build application and create golden AMI.
  2. Copy AMI to DR region and update AMI map.
  3. Update CloudFormation template reference and upload to DR S3 bucket.
  4. Run a scheduled test launch from DR AMI and run smoke tests.
Analogy
Treat the DR region like a fire extinguisher: it must be visible, charged, and tested regularly — not just stored in a box.
Concrete command pattern
# Example autoscaling update for Warm Standby (scaling up)
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name MyWarmStandbyASG \
  --desired-capacity 10 \
  --min-size 10 \
  --max-size 20 \
  --region us-east-1
A similar scripted pattern copies AMIs and updates template references. Always include a verification step that boots an instance from the copied AMI.
Common mistake
Assuming AMI copy implies environment parity. Remember to synchronize IAM, parameters, and secrets stores for the DR region as well.

screens.title: What is Warm Standby?
screens.narratorSegment: Warm Standby is a DR strategy that runs a minimal but functional version of your application in the DR region. Unlike Pilot Light, where compute is idle until activation, Warm Standby keeps a few instances and supporting services active so you can scale them up quickly if the primary fails. Data replication is still essential: RDS read replicas, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB Global Tables, and S3 replication ensure the DR copy has recent data. The main benefit is dramatically faster RTOs — often measured in minutes — at the cost of continuous run-rate expense. A concrete example from the chapter is running a small Auto Scaling Group with desired capacity one or two in the DR region. During failover you update the ASG desired capacity to production size and update Route 53 to point to the DR ALB. A common misconception is equating Warm Standby with active-active multi-region; Warm Standby is not necessarily active-active because the DR region often carries only a fraction of production capacity and is intended as a standby that can be scaled. The decision hinges on acceptable downtime and budget: choose Warm Standby when short RTOs justify the ongoing cost.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Warm Standby: a running, scaled-down application in DR that can be scaled up quickly to handle full traffic.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › What is Warm Standby?
Definition
Warm Standby keeps a reduced-capacity, fully functioning stack in the DR region. It receives replicated data and serves limited traffic until scaled up.
Why choose it
When your RTO must be very short and you are willing to pay for continuous, partial capacity in the DR region.
Key Takeaway

Warm Standby shortens recovery because the stack is already running; scale-up is the primary activation step.

Typical components
  • Scaled-down Auto Scaling Group with small instances.
  • Replicated database (Aurora Global Database or RDS read replica).
  • ALB and a small set of supporting services running.
Scaling example
aws autoscaling update-auto-scaling-group \
  --auto-scaling-group-name MyWarmStandbyASG \
  --desired-capacity 10 \
  --min-size 10 \
  --max-size 20 \
  --region us-east-1
Misconception
Warm Standby is not the same as active-active. It may run real traffic but typically at reduced capacity until you scale it to production levels.

screens.title: RTO, RPO and Cost: Pilot Light vs Warm Standby
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between Pilot Light and Warm Standby requires balancing recovery objectives against budget. Pilot Light typically yields RTOs in the tens of minutes range because you must launch compute and attach it to replicated data; RPOs depend on replication lag but are often in minutes when using read replicas or replication features. Pilot Light costs are low because you avoid running full compute continuously; the trade-off is activation time and orchestration complexity. Warm Standby reduces RTO to minutes and RPO to seconds or low minutes if you use low-latency replication like Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables, because much of the stack is already running. The cost is higher because you pay for running instances, networks, and some storage continuously in the DR region. A concrete scenario: if you require an RTO under five minutes and an RPO under one minute, Warm Standby with Aurora Global Database is the right fit; if you can tolerate a 30-minute outage and want to minimize cost, Pilot Light with an RDS read replica promoted on failover is more appropriate. Always include a cost estimate comparing hourly DR resource spend versus potential business impact of downtime when advising stakeholders.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off summary
keyIdea.text: Pilot Light: lower cost, longer RTO. Warm Standby: higher cost, faster RTO. Select based on business RTO/RPO and budget.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › RTO, RPO & Cost
Pilot Light
RTO: tens of minutes. RPO: minutes depending on replication. Cost: low ongoing due to minimal compute.
When to choose
Suitable when cost control matters and slightly longer recovery is acceptable, such as internal tools or non-critical workloads.
Warm Standby
RTO: minutes. RPO: seconds to minutes with fast replication features. Cost: higher because resources run continuously.
When to choose
Choose for public-facing apps or revenue-impacting systems where downtime must be minimal.
Example decision
Given an RTO of 30 minutes and RPO of 5 minutes: Pilot Light with RDS read replica and CloudFormation is suitable. Given RTO under 5 minutes and RPO under 1 minute: Warm Standby with Aurora Global Database and running ASGs is appropriate.

screens.title: Route 53 Failover Configuration
screens.narratorSegment: Route 53 failover routing provides DNS-level redirection when the primary endpoint fails health checks. The workflow is: create health checks for the primary and DR endpoints, create a failover record set that marks one record as PRIMARY and the other as SECONDARY, and enable EvaluateTargetHealth so Route 53 uses the ALB's health status when deciding where to route traffic. The chapter gives a CLI-oriented task to create two health checks for the ALBs in the primary and DR regions, then create a change-batch JSON that UPSERTs A records for app. example. com with set identifiers and failover flags. In practice you should design health check endpoints that return a synthetic success value, such as a /health path that performs quick checks of dependent services. A common mistake is relying on ALB DNS without health checks; if EvaluateTargetHealth is not set, Route 53 may not detect ALB backend failures rapidly. Also tune TTLs — shorter TTLs let clients switch faster but increase DNS query rates. Run a failover simulation in a test environment to verify the health check and change-batch behavior before relying on it in production.

narration.text: Route 53 failover routing provides DNS-level redirection when the primary endpoint fails health checks. The workflow is: create health checks for the primary and DR endpoints, create a failover record set that marks one record as PRIMARY and the other as SECONDARY, and enable EvaluateTargetHealth so Route 53 uses the ALB's health status when deciding where to route traffic. In practice you should design health check endpoints that return a synthetic success value, such as a /health path that performs quick checks of dependent services. A common mistake is relying on ALB DNS without health checks; if EvaluateTargetHealth is not set, Route 53 may not detect ALB backend failures rapidly. Also tune TTLs — shorter TTLs let clients switch faster but increase DNS query rates. Run a failover simulation in a test environment to verify the health check and change-batch behavior before relying on it in production.

keyIdea.title: Route 53 failover
keyIdea.text: Use health checks, PRIMARY/SECONDARY records, and EvaluateTargetHealth to automatically route to the DR ALB when the primary fails.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Route 53 Failover
Health check design
Use a dedicated /health endpoint on the ALB that performs a shallow check of critical dependencies. Keep the health check interval and thresholds conservative enough to avoid false positives but responsive enough to detect real failures.
Failover record pattern
Create two resource record sets with SetIdentifier values and Failover set to PRIMARY and SECONDARY respectively. Attach the corresponding HealthCheckId to each and set EvaluateTargetHealth to true on the AliasTarget.
CLI template excerpt
# Example snippet: create health check for ALB
aws route53 create-health-check \
  --caller-reference "primary-alb-health-check-$(date +%s)" \
  --health-check-config '{"FullyQualifiedDomainName":"primary-alb.us-west-2.elb.amazonaws.com", "Port":80, "Type":"HTTP", "ResourcePath":"/health", "RequestInterval":10, "FailureThreshold":3}'
Verification
Simulate primary failure in test environment and confirm Route 53 immediately begins resolving to the DR ALB according to TTL and health check timing.

screens.title: Data Replication Options
screens.narratorSegment: Robust data replication is the backbone of both Pilot Light and Warm Standby. The chapter outlines service-level choices: for relational databases, RDS read replicas in a DR region give you a promoted copy during failover. For very low RPO needs, Aurora Global Database provides fast cross-region replication optimized to deliver RPOs in seconds. For NoSQL, DynamoDB Global Tables provide active-active replication across regions. For object storage, S3 Cross-Region Replication keeps buckets synchronized. Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Data Replication
Relational options
RDS Read Replica: cross-region replica that can be promoted. Aurora Global Database: low-latency global replication designed for fast promotion and very low RPO.
NoSQL & objects
DynamoDB Global Tables offer multi-region active-active replication. S3 Cross-Region Replication keeps objects synchronized for recovery or rehydration.
Operational checks
  • Monitor replication lag and set thresholds for automated alerts.
  • Include replication verification in failover drills.
  • Ensure DR region secrets and parameter values are synchronized.
Concrete scenario
For RTO<5 minutes and RPO<1 minute: use Aurora Global Database for cross-region replication and a small running Warm Standby cluster that can be promoted and scaled.
Caveat
Replication alone is not enough — ensure configuration, network, and secrets are available in DR to allow services to start immediately after promotion.

screens.title: Testing, CI/CD, and Common Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Testing and automation are the difference between a theoretical DR plan and a reliable one. The chapter highlights two recurring issues: configuration drift between primary and DR artifacts and insufficient drill coverage. Your CI/CD pipeline must copy AMIs, update CloudFormation templates in the DR region, and synchronize parameter and secret values. Schedule regular failover drills that simulate full primary-region loss and run through the entire activation sequence: promote replicas, create stacks, scale or launch instances, update DNS, and run smoke tests. During drills, isolate the DR environment to prevent accidental impacts to production and validate telemetry such as replication lag, instance health, and service responses. Common pitfalls include leaving long TTLs on DNS records, neglecting EvaluateTargetHealth, or failing to test IAM roles and network routes in the DR region. A practical test: run a timed drill to measure actual RTO and RPO against targets; if you miss targets, iterate on automation steps and tuning. The goal is not only to pass a single drill, but to create reproducible, automated runs your team can execute confidently during an incident. content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Testing & Pitfalls
Drill checklist
  • Promote DR database and confirm write capability.
  • Deploy CloudFormation stack in DR and launch instances from DR AMIs.
  • Update Route 53 failover records and validate client routing behavior.
  • Run smoke tests and measure end-to-end RTO and RPO.
CI/CD integration
Have pipelines that automatically copy AMIs, upload templates to DR S3, and rotate DR environment variables as part of each release cycle.
Common mistakes
  • Not testing full failover end-to-end.
  • Out-of-sync CloudFormation templates or AMIs in DR.
  • Long DNS TTLs and not using EvaluateTargetHealth.
Pro tip
Create an automated timed drill that fails if RTO or RPO objectives are not met; use the results to prioritize automation work.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These three core concepts capture the practical decisions you'll make when designing DR. First, Pilot Light keeps data and deployment artifacts ready while compute is launched on demand, reducing cost but increasing activation time. Second, Warm Standby runs a scaled-down application stack continuously in the DR region, offering much faster recovery at higher ongoing cost. Keep these points in mind as you design or audit a DR plan: replication strategy must match your RPO, artifacts must be synchronized, and DNS health checks must be tuned so failover behaves predictably. Replication = RPO
Choose replication tech that meets your data-loss tolerance.
Readiness = RTO
Decide whether compute runs in DR (Warm Standby) or is launched on demand (Pilot Light).

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn two practical AWS disaster recovery strategies that sit between full cold backup and fully active multi-region setups. Pilot Light keeps core data and artifacts replicated to a secondary region while compute is launched on demand; Warm Standby runs a minimally scaled, working version of your application in the DR region that you can scale up quickly. We'll look at the specific services you rely on — cross-region RDS replicas, DynamoDB Global Tables, S3 replication, AMIs, CloudFormation templates, Auto Scaling, and Route 53 failover routing — and how they change recovery time objective and recovery point objective trade-offs. You will see concrete CLI examples for stack creation, autoscaling updates, and Route 53 change batches, and learn common mistakes such as out-of-sync templates or failing to test end-to-end. By the end, you should be able to choose which strategy fits an application's RTO/RPO targets and budget, know the activation steps for each approach, and understand which parts of your architecture must be continuously replicated. Consider how short your acceptable outage window is, then ask: is it worth paying for always-on compute in the DR region, or do I accept a slightly longer activation for much lower cost?

These four objectives map directly to real DR tasks you'll perform in AWS. First, you will design and implement a Pilot Light architecture, which means you must know how to create AMIs, store CloudFormation templates in the DR region, and set up continuous data replication for services like RDS or DynamoDB. Second, you'll design and implement a Warm Standby setup: that includes provisioning and maintaining a scaled-down, running application in the DR region and knowing how to scale it up quickly. Third, you'll compare RTO, RPO, and cost trade-offs between the two strategies so you can recommend the right approach for an application's recovery targets. Fourth, you'll configure Route 53 failover routing with health checks so that DNS automatically redirects traffic to the DR region when the primary fails. Each objective includes a practical milestone so you can verify competency during a drill or in hands-on labs.

Let's unpack the milestones so you know how to verify each objective. For Pilot Light, your milestone is to have an RDS read replica or equivalent replicated dataset in the DR region, AMIs copied to the DR region, and a CloudFormation template stored and able to create the application stack that attaches to the DR database. Test this by doing a controlled activation and validating the application connects to the promoted database. For Warm Standby, your milestone is a running, but scaled-down, application in the DR region that serves real traffic; validate by scaling up the Auto Scaling Group and confirming the application handles synthetic load. For RTO and RPO comparison, your milestone is an estimation table showing expected activation times and data loss windows for both strategies using your real replication metrics. For Route 53 failover, create health checks pointing at ALBs and a failover record set that flips to the DR endpoint when the primary fails. Each milestone should be proven by a runbook you can execute during a DR drill.

Pilot Light is a disaster recovery approach where you keep the minimal, critical pieces of your system always ready in the DR region while leaving the bulk of compute turned off to save cost. The key claim is simple: continuously replicate your essential data services and keep deployment artifacts ready, then launch compute and networking on demand during an incident. A concrete example is keeping an Amazon RDS read replica in the DR region or using DynamoDB Global Tables to keep data synchronized, while AMIs and CloudFormation templates for application servers are copied and available. When the primary region fails, you promote the replica or restore from replicated snapshots, create the application stack from templates, launch EC2 instances from the AMIs, and update Route 53 to route traffic to the newly created ALB. A common misconception is that Pilot Light is a backup schedule; it is not. Backups are point-in-time copies, while Pilot Light requires continuous replication and pre-built infrastructure artifacts so activation is deliberate and time-bounded. In practice you must automate AMI creation and template synchronization, and run regular drills to validate that the runbook performs as expected. Think of Pilot Light as holding the spark and tools in place so you can light the full furnace quickly when needed.

Activating a Pilot Light setup is a coordinated set of steps that must be automated where possible. The flow begins with ensuring data is ready — promote a read replica or restore a recent cross-region snapshot so your DR database is a writable primary. Next, deploy the pre-stored CloudFormation template which creates the compute, networking, and load balancing resources. Launch EC2 instances from your pre-built AMIs so configuration and dependencies are already installed. Once instances are registered with the new Application Load Balancer, update environment variables and connection strings to point to the DR database endpoint. Finally, update Route 53 failover records so traffic resolves to the DR ALB. A concrete CLI example from the chapter shows creating a CloudFormation stack using an app-stack. yaml template and then applying a Route 53 change-batch that UPSERTs A records pointing to the DR ALB. A common misconception is that you can skip DNS TTL tuning; without short TTLs and proper EvaluateTargetHealth settings, clients may continue to hit the failed primary. Always include a post-activation verification step: smoke tests and health checks to ensure the application is fully operational before declaring recovery complete.

A reliable Pilot Light or Warm Standby depends on up-to-date AMIs and infrastructure-as-code templates in the DR region. Automation in your CI/CD pipeline should produce AMIs when application builds succeed and then copy those AMIs to the DR region, and also update CloudFormation templates or S3-stored artifacts that the DR stack will read. The chapter emphasizes that failing to synchronize templates or AMIs is a common cause of DR activation failure. Concretely, your pipeline can run image creation, then run a cross-region copy, and finally upload or version the CloudFormation template in the DR bucket. A test you should automate is launching an instance from the DR AMI periodically and running an application smoke test. That verifies both the AMI content and the networking/security settings. A misconception is assuming that copying AMIs is sufficient: you must also ensure IAM roles, parameter store entries, and environment variables needed in the DR region are kept in sync. The practical result is a runbook that states: build AMI, copy AMI to DR, update template S3 version, and run a test launch — all triggered automatically by a successful mainline release.

Warm Standby is a DR strategy that runs a minimal but functional version of your application in the DR region. Unlike Pilot Light, where compute is idle until activation, Warm Standby keeps a few instances and supporting services active so you can scale them up quickly if the primary fails. Data replication is still essential: RDS read replicas, Aurora Global Database, DynamoDB Global Tables, and S3 replication ensure the DR copy has recent data. The main benefit is dramatically faster RTOs — often measured in minutes — at the cost of continuous run-rate expense. A concrete example from the chapter is running a small Auto Scaling Group with desired capacity one or two in the DR region. During failover you update the ASG desired capacity to production size and update Route 53 to point to the DR ALB. A common misconception is equating Warm Standby with active-active multi-region; Warm Standby is not necessarily active-active because the DR region often carries only a fraction of production capacity and is intended as a standby that can be scaled. The decision hinges on acceptable downtime and budget: choose Warm Standby when short RTOs justify the ongoing cost.

Choosing between Pilot Light and Warm Standby requires balancing recovery objectives against budget. Pilot Light typically yields RTOs in the tens of minutes range because you must launch compute and attach it to replicated data; RPOs depend on replication lag but are often in minutes when using read replicas or replication features. Pilot Light costs are low because you avoid running full compute continuously; the trade-off is activation time and orchestration complexity. Warm Standby reduces RTO to minutes and RPO to seconds or low minutes if you use low-latency replication like Aurora Global Database or DynamoDB Global Tables, because much of the stack is already running. The cost is higher because you pay for running instances, networks, and some storage continuously in the DR region. A concrete scenario: if you require an RTO under five minutes and an RPO under one minute, Warm Standby with Aurora Global Database is the right fit; if you can tolerate a 30-minute outage and want to minimize cost, Pilot Light with an RDS read replica promoted on failover is more appropriate. Always include a cost estimate comparing hourly DR resource spend versus potential business impact of downtime when advising stakeholders.

The workflow is: create health checks for the primary and DR endpoints, create a failover record set that marks one record as PRIMARY and the other as SECONDARY, and enable EvaluateTargetHealth so Route 53 uses the ALB's health status when deciding where to route traffic. The chapter gives a CLI-oriented task to create two health checks for the ALBs in the primary and DR regions, then create a change-batch JSON that UPSERTs A records for app. example. com with set identifiers and failover flags. In practice you should design health check endpoints that return a synthetic success value, such as a /health path that performs quick checks of dependent services. A common mistake is relying on ALB DNS without health checks; if EvaluateTargetHealth is not set, Route 53 may not detect ALB backend failures rapidly. Also tune TTLs — shorter TTLs let clients switch faster but increase DNS query rates.
